sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Sarcodon imbricatus (L.) P. Karst. is a terrestrial tooth fungus. Its cap, usually 6–22 cm across in a recent description, starts convex and flattens, often becoming depressed at the center. The yellowish-brown surface bears coarse scales with raised tips; the scales are initially close in color to the background and darken to brown with age. The older name Hydnum imbricatum L. is its basionym.

sections.title: Spines, stem and flesh
sections.text: The underside bears crowded, decurrent spines, never gills or pores: they are grayish white when young, pale gray at maturity, and may turn brown when touched; a recent study measured them to about 9 mm long. The pale stem is usually eccentric, about 2.5–6 cm long, and may turn brownish or greenish when touched. The flesh is grayish white. Taste descriptions differ: mild in the recent taxonomic study, but slightly bitter after a few minutes in a regional synthesis. Taste is therefore not a constant character. The smell becomes more pronounced on drying, and the spore print is brownish.

sections.title: Habitat and similar species
sections.text: It grows on the ground in mycorrhizal association with conifers, especially spruce (Picea); specimens have also been reported in forests with both fir and spruce. Fruiting is in late summer and autumn. Older records from pine may refer to Sarcodon squamosus: a molecular and morphological study separated that pine-associated species from spruce-associated S. imbricatus. Cap color and scales alone may not be enough to identify a specimen.

sections.title: Edibility and caution
sections.text: The VAPKO list of edible mushrooms presented includes S. imbricatus. This is not foraging advice or an identification: tooth fungi can resemble one another, and characters vary. Never eat a wild mushroom based only on an image.

traits: Cap 6–22 cm across, convex then flattening, often depressed in the center, yellowish brown with coarse raised scales that darken with age
Crowded, decurrent spines, grayish white then pale gray, sometimes browning when touched, up to about 9 mm long; no gills or pores
Pale, usually eccentric stem about 2.5–6 cm long, sometimes turning brownish or greenish when touched
Grayish-white flesh; taste reported as mild or becoming slightly bitter depending on sources; smell stronger when dried
On the ground beneath conifers, especially spruce; late summer and autumn
safetyNote: The VAPKO list of edible mushrooms presented includes Sarcodon imbricatus. Taste reports vary, and consumption requires certain identification; never eat a wild mushroom based only on a photo. If symptoms occur after ingestion, contact a poison centre or emergency services immediately.
